Abdullah: A Story of an Age Awakening to Itself

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-11-19

Reading Kazi Imdadul Haque’s Abdullah feels like someone has opened a window in my mind. It brings me face to face with a society in which people place greater trust in inherited customs than in their own judgment, clinging to superstition rather than reason. Exploitation thrives under the guise of spiritual allegiance to religious preceptors. Religious orthodoxy constrains freedom of thought, while ordinary people accept these conditions as simply the natural order of life. Into this society steps a young man named Abdullah, asking a deceptively simple question: Why? Why should people not think for themselves? Why must everything be accepted simply because it is old? Why must society continue in this way? These questions may sound ordinary enough, but in the world Abdullah inhabits, the very act of asking them requires courage. I have come to feel that the entire novel is an exploration of this one question, expressed in different forms. Abdullah’s personal struggles, the conflicts within his family, his ideas about education and his resistance to social injustice—all ultimately lead back to the same question: will people ever learn to think for themselves?

I do not see Abdullah merely as a character; I see him as a question embodied. After his father's death, he is forced to abandon his studies and seek employment. Yet the questioning mind within him refuses to come to a halt. Looking around, he sees people who have lost the habit of thinking for themselves. They follow religious preceptors unquestioningly, place their faith in amulets and charms, and rarely stop to ask why. Abdullah cannot accept this habit of surrendering one's own judgment and allowing others to dictate how one should live. He searches for reason, remains attentive to human suffering, and it is here that his struggle begins. Nor does that struggle end at home. His wife, Saleha, is shaped by inherited customs, while Abdullah is drawn towards new ideas. I would not describe their differences as ordinary marital disagreements. They are, in fact, two different eras confronting each other within the walls of a single home. Here, too, the same question returns: must people surrender themselves to the habits of the past, or can they learn to think independently?

One of the most heartbreaking episodes in the novel is the story of Madan Gazi, a peasant from Palashdanga. Caught in a web of debt, he gradually loses his land. Eventually, he is forced to sell even the homestead he calls his own. This cannot be dismissed as the misfortune of a single family. The impoverishment and dispossession of rural peasants in Bengal have continued across generations, and the story is far from over. Imdadul Haque portrays this reality with such sensitivity that the weight of it settles heavily on the reader. A question inevitably arises: how can someone who spends an entire lifetime clinging to the soil eventually lose even the right to call that soil his own? Yet even in the midst of such helplessness, Abdullah stands beside Madan. Mir Mohsen Ali, a middle-class man, also extends a helping hand, even if from a distance. These moments remind me that the capacity for compassion is still alive in people. Not everyone may know how to question injustice, and not everyone may find the courage to resist it. But the simple willingness to stand beside another human being is itself no small force in the making of a different society.

The political currents set in motion by the Partition of Bengal in 1905 also find their way into the novel. The Swadeshi movement reaches Rasul­pur High School, bringing with it calls to buy indigenous goods and boycott foreign products. These were more than acts of political protest; they marked the emergence of a new social consciousness. Yet Imdadul Haque makes it clear that learning to think differently comes at a price. A teacher loses his job, government surveillance intensifies, and unrest spreads through the school. Reading these episodes today, I find little that is surprising. The tendency to use education in the service of particular interests remains very much with us. Abdullah, however, refuses to be discouraged. He engages a maulvi to teach Persian, promotes indigenous sports, and refuses to confine education to the pages of textbooks. To him, education is about shaping people and teaching them to understand the world around them. These initiatives may seem modest, but that is often how change begins. One person learns to think differently, and gradually others begin to follow. For Abdullah, this transformation seems to matter more than anything else.

The episode surrounding his father-in-law's illness is, to me, one of the most powerful sections of the novel. A man falls seriously ill, and the entire family is anxious to see him recover. But disagreement soon emerges over how he should be treated. Some place their trust in traditional hakims, seek the blessings of the pir, and turn to amulets for protection. Abdullah and his brother, Abdul Kader, stand on the other side, arguing for modern medical treatment. The question here is not simply which form of medicine people choose to trust. It is something more fundamental: when someone falls ill, should we rely on habit and inherited belief, or should we make decisions guided by reason and necessity? Around one sick man, two different ways of seeing the world seem to confront each other within the same household. There is financial pressure, emotional uncertainty and distrust among family members. The resulting crisis feels so vividly real that, as I read, I find myself almost inside that house. It is painful to witness, yet impossible to look away. For what we see here is not merely the helplessness of one family, but a deeply rooted pattern in our society.

The events within Syed Sahib's family also give me much to think about. Through Saleha's experiences in the village and Abdullah's eventual rise to the position of headmaster, we begin to see how change gradually finds its way into family life. It is easy to speak of transforming society from the outside; bringing that transformation into one's own home is far more difficult. The attempt to introduce modern education into the madrasa, and the resistance it encounters from the pirs, bring this difficulty into sharp focus. The tension between inherited tradition and new ways of thinking repeatedly comes to the surface. I feel that Imdadul Haque is suggesting something important here: no society changes overnight. One generation struggles against established beliefs, habits and institutions to open a path; the next carries that effort a little further. The disagreements surrounding religious customs and practices associated with the mosque raise the same question once again: should everything we have come to practise in the name of religious belief remain beyond question? Or should reason and independent judgment have their rightful place alongside faith?

There is something about Imdadul Haque's writing that I particularly admire. He does not tell Abdullah's story alone; he gives such careful attention to the people around him that the small community of Rasul­pur gradually comes alive before our eyes. We encounter religious institutions, class divisions, strained family relationships, human vulnerability and self-interest. Together, they reveal the social fabric of an entire period. The author exposes human failings without diminishing the people who embody them. There is protest in his writing, but never an unnecessary harshness. He does not seek to establish his position by simply condemning others. Instead, through people's behaviour, beliefs and struggles, he allows us to recognise where the problems lie. To me, this is one of the greatest strengths of his writing. For when we speak of social change, it is not enough simply to reject the old. We must also try to understand why those old beliefs have taken such deep root in people's lives. Imdadul Haque makes that effort. And it is here that Abdullah moves beyond the boundaries of an ordinary narrative to reveal the deeper truths of the society it portrays.

One of the greatest strengths of Abdullah is that the novel never tries to make itself seem more important than it is. It tells its story in a simple, unassuming way. To me, it is an honest novel. It exposes the failings of society and makes a case for change, yet never tries to force a particular conclusion upon the reader. When young people like Abdullah begin to question established customs, cracks gradually appear in the thick ice of a society long resistant to change. Change does not come easily. It has to make its way through obstacles and resistance. But it does come. That is why Abdullah cannot be dismissed as merely the story of a family or a village. Through it, we glimpse an entire society at a particular moment in history. And within that society, we begin to see a different kind of dream taking shape for the next generation: a world in which people think for themselves, pursue education, treat others with humanity, and refuse to accept everything blindly.

Reading the novel today, I am repeatedly struck by the thought that Imdadul Haque was writing about his own time, yet many of the problems he described remain unresolved. Religious orthodoxy persists, superstition continues, and people are still influenced and exploited in the name of pir-murid relationships. Society has changed, and so have people's ways of life, but those changes have not always reached the way people think. Abdullah's questions, therefore, continue to confront us. Have we learned to think for ourselves? Are we willing to examine our beliefs in the light of reason? Have we truly made education and humanity part of our lives? As I search for answers to these questions, I find myself returning to one thought: Abdullah's story is still our story. For as long as people need reason, humanity and education, Imdadul Haque's novel will remain relevant. To me, Abdullah is not simply the story of one man's awakening. It is a testament to an entire society's longing to awaken.
